body:
Why extraction may not produce pure metal

After extraction, a metal may still contain other metals and unwanted substances. Refining removes impurities so that the metal becomes suitable for applications requiring higher purity.

One widely used method is electrolytic refining. Copper provides the standard school-level example. The same general method can be used for several other metals.

Electrolytic refining of copper

The arrangement contains 3 essential components:

  • Anode: A block of impure copper, connected to the positive terminal.
  • Cathode: A thin sheet of pure copper, connected to the negative terminal.
  • Electrolyte: A suitable copper salt solution, commonly acidified copper sulphate solution.

When electric current passes through the arrangement, copper from the impure anode enters the solution as copper ions. Copper ions from the solution gain electrons at the cathode and are deposited as copper metal.

As the process continues, the impure anode becomes smaller and pure copper accumulates at the cathode.

What happens to impurities?

Different impurities behave differently. Some soluble impurities remain in the electrolyte. Insoluble impurities settle beneath the anode and form anode mud.

The presence of anode mud is therefore not the same as copper deposition. The desired refined metal is collected at the cathode, whereas insoluble impurities collect separately.

Extraction electrolysis versus refining electrolysis

FeatureElectrolytic extractionElectrolytic refining
Main purposeObtain metal from its compoundPurify previously obtained metal
Typical exampleSodium from molten NaClCopper from impure copper
ElectrolyteSuitable molten compoundSuitable metal salt solution
Cathode resultNew metal is producedPure metal is deposited

Both processes use electrical energy and involve reactions at electrodes, but their starting materials and purposes are different. Extraction produces metal from a compound. Refining increases the purity of metal that has already been extracted.

Prelims focus

  • In copper refining, the impure copper block is the anode.
  • The pure copper sheet is the cathode.
  • Acidified copper sulphate solution is the electrolyte.
  • Pure copper is deposited at the cathode.
  • Insoluble impurities settle as anode mud.
  • Trap: The cathode is the site of pure-metal deposition, not the collection point for anode mud.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Section 3.4.6, pp. 52–53.]

title: Electrolytic Refining of Metals

body:
What corrosion means

Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal through chemical reactions with substances in its surroundings, such as oxygen, water and other atmospheric components.

Corrosion affects the appearance and durability of metal articles. It can damage gates, railings, vehicles, pipes and other objects. However, corrosion does not always produce the same colour or compound.

Rusting of iron

Rusting is a familiar form of corrosion specific to iron and iron-containing materials. Iron exposed to moist air forms a reddish-brown, flaky substance called rust.

Rust is mainly hydrated iron(III) oxide, commonly represented as Fe2O3·xH2O. Its exact water content can vary.

Conditions needed for rusting

Both oxygen and water are needed for ordinary rusting of iron. Dry air alone does not cause iron to rust in the same way, and water with oxygen excluded does not produce the usual rusting reaction.

Humidity increases the availability of moisture. Dissolved salts can accelerate corrosion, which is why unprotected iron structures may deteriorate more rapidly in coastal environments.

Corrosion of other metals

MetalCommon surface changeMain explanation
IronReddish-brown rustFormation of hydrated iron oxides
SilverBlack tarnishFormation of silver sulphide, Ag2S
CopperGreen coatingFormation of basic copper carbonate in moist air containing CO2
AluminiumThin oxide layerAdherent Al2O3 slows further oxidation

Silver is often described as a noble or relatively unreactive metal, but it can still tarnish because it reacts with sulphur-containing substances in air. Low reactivity does not mean that a metal can never undergo any surface reaction.

Preventing corrosion

Painting, oiling and greasing

A protective coating can prevent moisture and oxygen from contacting the metal. Paint is suitable for many exposed iron articles, while oil or grease may protect suitable moving or stored metal parts.

These coatings must remain effective. If a barrier is damaged, the newly exposed metal may begin to corrode.

Galvanisation

Galvanisation is the protection of iron or steel by coating it with zinc. The zinc layer prevents direct exposure of the iron surface to the surroundings.

Zinc is more reactive than iron. It can therefore provide additional protection even where the coating is locally damaged. This explains why a zinc coating is particularly useful for iron pipes, sheets and other articles exposed to moisture.

Electroplating and chromium coating

A metal can also be protected by depositing a coating of another metal. Chromium plating may improve appearance and surface resistance, while other protective coatings serve different practical purposes.

Anodising

Anodising is used especially with aluminium. It increases the thickness of the protective aluminium oxide layer, improving resistance to further corrosion.

Alloying

Changing the composition of a metal can improve its corrosion resistance. For example, stainless steel contains iron with chromium and commonly nickel. The chromium helps the material resist rusting by forming a protective surface film.

Galvanisation and anodising are different: galvanisation adds a zinc coating to iron or steel; anodising thickens the protective oxide layer on aluminium.

Prelims focus

  • Rusting of iron requires both oxygen and water.
  • Salt-containing moisture can accelerate corrosion.
  • Silver develops black silver sulphide tarnish.
  • Copper develops a green coating of basic copper carbonate.
  • Galvanisation uses zinc; anodising strengthens the aluminium oxide layer.
  • Trap: A protective oxide layer on aluminium is not equivalent to the loose rust coating on iron.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 1, Chemical Reactions and Equations, Section 1.3.1, p. 13; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Sections 3.5–3.5.1, pp. 53–54; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 6, Physical and Chemical Changes, Section 6.3, pp. 63–64.]

pictures.caption: Moist, salt-containing air can accelerate corrosion of exposed iron.

title: Corrosion of Metals and Methods of Prevention

body:
What is an alloy?

An alloy is a mixture of 2 or more elements, at least 1 of which is a metal, made to obtain useful properties. It may contain 2 or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal.

Alloys are commonly prepared by combining suitable constituents in the molten state and allowing the material to solidify. At the school level, alloys are usually described as homogeneous mixtures.

An alloy is not necessarily a compound. Its constituents need not be present in the fixed atomic proportions characteristic of a chemical compound. Changing the proportions of the constituents can change the alloy's properties.

Why alloys are made

Pure metals do not always possess the most suitable combination of strength, hardness, corrosion resistance and melting behaviour. Adding other elements can modify these properties.

For example, pure iron is relatively soft. Adding a controlled amount of carbon can make it harder and stronger. Adding chromium and other suitable elements can improve the corrosion resistance of iron-based alloys.

The exact effect depends on the constituents and their proportions. It is therefore inaccurate to say that every alloy is necessarily harder, more conductive or lower-melting than every pure metal.

Important alloys and their constituents

AlloyMain constituentsCharacteristic or use
BrassCopper + zincUseful for fittings, utensils and decorative articles
BronzeCopper + tinUsed in statues, bells and other articles
SteelIron + carbonStronger and harder than pure iron in many useful forms
Stainless steelIron + chromium; often nickel and carbonResists corrosion; used in utensils and equipment
Traditional solderTin + leadLow-melting joining alloy
Gold jewellery alloyGold + copper or silverHarder than very pure gold

Brass versus bronze

Brass and bronze both contain copper, but their second main constituents differ:

  • Brass: Copper and zinc.
  • Bronze: Copper and tin.

This distinction is useful because both may have similar appearances and practical applications. Appearance alone is not a reliable way to identify their compositions.

Steel versus stainless steel

Ordinary steel is mainly an iron-carbon alloy. Stainless steel contains chromium as an important additional constituent and often contains nickel. Its improved corrosion resistance is associated especially with the protective surface film formed by chromium.

Stainless steel is corrosion-resistant, not absolutely incapable of corrosion under every possible condition.

Amalgams

An amalgam is an alloy containing mercury. The defining feature is the presence of mercury, not the presence of copper, iron or gold.

Alloy versus ionic compound

FeatureAlloyTypical ionic compound
NatureMixtureChemical compound
CompositionCan vary within the alloy systemFixed ratio of ions in its formula
ExampleBrassNaCl
Electrical behaviourMany conduct in solid formSolid ionic compounds do not ordinarily conduct

Prelims focus

  • Brass = copper + zinc.
  • Bronze = copper + tin.
  • Steel = mainly iron + carbon.
  • Stainless steel contains chromium and commonly nickel.
  • Traditional solder contains tin and lead.
  • Amalgam means an alloy containing mercury.
  • Trap: Alloys are mixtures; an ionic compound such as NaCl has a fixed ionic composition.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Section 3.5.1, p. 54; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 6, Physical and Chemical Changes, p. 64.]
